items.title: Formlabs Form Studio 1 Teardown
items.author: bunnie
items.content:
Formlabs has recently launched the Form Studio 1. I’ve had fun tearing down every new generation of their printers. I am pleased to continue that tradition, and to share the joy of learning by taking apart someone else’s product.

Financial interest disclosure: Formlabs provided me with the printer for this teardown, with no contingencies on the contents or views expressed in this post. I am also a shareholder of Formlabs.

The Form Studio 1 picks up where the Form 4 SLA printer leaves off. For details, you can review the teardown of the Form 4. The key point is that the Form 4 represented a watershed moment in Formlabs’ evolution from a galvanometer based printer to an LCD shutter based printer. The basic architecture of the Form 4, and the Form Studio 1, is reviewed in the diagram below.

While the architecture of the Form Studio 1 mirrors that of the Form 4, the Form Studio 1 retails at roughly a quarter the price of a Form 4. This addresses one of the biggest pain points about the Formlabs printer line-up: the high base price of the printer. Since a big theme of the Form Studio 1 is cost reduction, let’s first explore some of the cost drivers in building products like printers.

Complex electromechanical systems are expensive to assemble. The main driver is the cost of labor: a screw costs a fraction of a cent; the labor to install the screw is far larger. Furthermore, there is a big difference in the skills required between a person who only puts one screw into a single hole all day long, and someone who has to keep track of a fifty-step build, routing cables from a diverse number of endpoints, while attaching screws with the correct amount of torque and possibly other bespoke requirements such as thread lockers. A good production-line setup can go a long way to fool-proof the build process – e.g. pre-kitting parts, kanban systems, etc. – but these systems also cost money to set up and run, and the overhead only becomes negligible at the highest volumes.

For complex, high-BOM cost builds, the cost of rework is also an important consideration. The high cost of materials means it’s almost never acceptable to simply scrap defective assemblies. However, complex builds have a low net yield, especially in the early phase of the production ramp. The statistics are daunting: a 50-step build where each step is 99% reliable would only yield 60% good product; at 100 steps, you’re well under 40% yield. Worse yet, the problem is often going to be a single subtle issue in just one step out of many, so you’re left looking for a needle in a haystack. This type of task requires the expertise of a senior technician, who bills at a higher rate.

Thus, the most effective way to reduce cost is to simply design it out. One metric I can use to compare the Form Studio 1 to the Form 4 is how long it took to do the teardown. The Form 4 took me almost two solid weeks, on and off, of trying to figure out how all the parts came together. When I do a teardown, I try to envision the production flow and reverse it. The Form 4 had several forks in the process that I had to experiment with before I figured out a clean reverse flow. Even then, there were a couple assemblies whose build order I could not figure out. Eventually I gave up, and just tore them apart with brute force.

In contrast, the bulk of the Form Studio 1 took me about two afternoons to tear down. The inverse flow was intuitive. At a minimum, this is a strong indicator that rework costs were more manageable.

Improved Design for Manufacturing

This design improvement was driven in part by the choice to use a cast aluminum plate as the reference point for everything in the build. It is a solid chunk of metal with many complicated features molded into it, followed up by two CNC machining passes (one for each side) where critical surfaces are leveled, high-precision holes are drilled out, and alignment bosses are refined. Below is an overview picture of the base plate.

The image below more clearly shows the CNC machined surfaces and drilled holes.

Note the machining marks on the slightly raised surfaces in the casting. A small amount of extra material is roughly placed during the casting process in these areas, and then a precision CNC pass refines it into an accurate, smooth surface.

This is in contrast to the Form 4, which assembles a rigid box out of multiple sheet metal and polymer parts. The machining tolerance of each of these sub-assemblies has to be carefully controlled, and often jigs are required during the build process to ensure tolerances.

The way for an electrical engineer to think about this is that a cast aluminum plate is to a sheet metal build-up as a solid copper ground plane on a circuit board is to multiple isolated circuit boards cabled together (cast aluminum : sheet metal build-up :: single ground plane : multiple circuit boards; do they even teach analogies anymore in grade school, or is this just me showing my age?).

When designing a circuit board, using a solid sheet of copper on an inner layer for ground allows one great freedom to use single wires to connect chips. However, if you separate the grounds, or if you are routing between two separate circuit boards, differences in ground references reduce noise margins. One needs to pay attention to either lining up the grounds (e.g. with lots of explicit ground ties) or making misaligned grounds not a problem (e.g. using differential pairs, etc.). This comes at the cost of more expensive connectors, more wires, or both.

In mechanical design, the same reference problem exists. While it is trivial to say that a given beam is X centimeters long, that’s not the parameter that matters – what you care about is often not the height of a single hole above the base plate, but the height of the hole relative to the shaft that feeds into it. If both the hole and shaft are mounted on the same base plate, then any error in the base plate thickness cancels out. If the hole and shaft are mounted on separate plates, then any error in the alignment of the respective base plates adds to the tolerance.

Mechanical systems are disadvantaged compared to electrical systems in terms of tolerance margins because in electronics we have an exponential in the device equations to drive noise margins to the rail at every stage of logic. However, mechanical systems generally have linear transfer curves, so tolerances stack additively throughout the build. Thus it is even more important to be aware of where your reference geometry is and to make sure it is faithfully communicated or preserved throughout the assembly. A single cast metal base part largely solves this problem by collapsing it into a single dimensionally stable part.

The trade-off of using a cast aluminum base plate is that the molds for casting are quite expensive, which makes design revisions and tweaks correspondingly more difficult. However, the Form Studio 1 re-uses much of the Form 4 light architecture, and so the engineering team could take a clear-eyed look at the design, curating features from a much smaller design space than if they were trying to simultaneously revise the light architecture and do a cost down in the same design generation.

Improving Cost, Starting with the Unboxing Experience

Another cost driver in large systems is logistics. The sheer bulk and complexity of inventorying components, storing them, and moving them adds up. Anyone who has experienced Ikea furniture absorbs this lesson indirectly. Ikea can warehouse fifty shelves in the space of a single show floor demo shelf, reducing warehousing and retail costs. In general, more compact products are cheaper to produce and sell.

It also turns out that there is an optimal density for shipping based on modality. For air freight, that density is in the range of 0.16-0.2 grams/cc. This is why all mobile phone boxes are about the same size – there’s a certain net density target for air shipments that the manufacturers are looking to hit, and tuning the box size is one way to achieve that.

According to Formlabs’ product data, the box is 107,525 cubic centimeters and weighs about 18,500 grams. That’s 0.17 grams/cc – exactly at the sweet spot for air shipping. In contrast, the Form 4 was 0.11 grams/cc. This means that even though the box only weighed 23kg, they were paying a rate to ship a 34kg product, because the box contained too much dead air.

That 11kg difference adds up – assuming they are paying around \$10/kg (costs vary, but the rate is in the range of \$3-12/kg depending on volume and broker), that’s a \$100 extra cost for shipping due to having the wrong product density. Given that the Form Studio 1 starts at \$699, adding \$100 for shipping dead air significantly erodes gross margins, and thus it would make sense to pay attention to this detail.

In previous Form printers, the build platform and resin tank were shipped separately, leaving the printer’s build volume as dead air inside its box. In the case of the Form Studio 1, I can see the extra attention to detail in total supply chain cost. The build platform and resin tank are packaged the dead air volume of the product, thus improving density and helping them hit the magic density for optimal air shipping.

A notable feature of every Formlabs product is the inclusion of 3D printed parts in mass production. In this case, the maintenance kit and a port cover are 3D printed.

In the case of the plug, it’s explicitly advertised as a 3D printed part; for the maintenance kit, I am only assuming it is, based on the texture and material feel. The plug in this case looks like it was optimized for a zero-post-process build: one end is flatted to stick to the build platform, and angled in such a way that the build proceeds without any support material. This leads to a nice product finish with minimal extra cost, in contrast to the previous plug on the Form 4:

Despite the focus on reducing costs, some features improved compared to previous generations. For example, the build platform got a nice redesign to include integrated supports.

The build platform itself has an interesting new detail to it. The texture of the surface now has a micromachined texture, probably done with a laser.

I’m not sure of all the reasons for the microtexturing, but there are three I can think of:

  1. Minimizing the impact of small scratches on the build platform surface. The platform inevitably accumulates a variety of small scratches from scraping models off, and these tend to become defect sites for future builds.
  2. Improving release of the model. It might just be me, or it might be the improved scraper, but the items seemed to come off more easily with this texturing.
  3. Removing the resin stirrer from the design.

The last point is the most speculative, but the Form Studio 1 loses a key mechanism from the Form 4: the resin stirring bar. The resin stirrer was not cheap – it required a fast, precise motor with an optical shaft encoder capable of whipping the stirring bar across the tank at high speeds. I don’t recall where I heard this rumor from, but I seem to remember that mixing with air had some property relevant to the chemistry of the resin, which is part of the reason why the stirrer was necessary. The stir bar also kept the resin evenly mixed helped mix the resin during tank filling and heating, but this is handled by gently churning the build platform up and down within the resin pool instead.

So, one possibility is that the microtexturing traps small amounts of air, which allows the stirrer to be costed out. I would emphasize that this is really just my speculation, but in the end, somehow Formlabs was able to cost-out the resin stirrer without loss of quality.

Another notable but simple quality of life improvement is the highly improved scraper bundled in the product. Previous generations’ scrapers were probably just a random paint scraper bought at the lowest cost – they were dull, flexed under use, and eventually rusted. The scraper included with the Form Studio 1 is serious business.

This seems to be a full custom product, with the Formlabs logo emblazoned on it. The scraper body is made of much thicker steel, and the edge is sharpened to a point. Its build quality makes it border on a martial apparatus, but it functions so well I’m tempted to get more just for other scraping applications around the home.

Before taking the Form Studio 1 apart, I repeated a test that I did on the Form 4 for light uniformity, where I put a piece of paper over the LCD panel and had it print a cleaning sheet, while taking a photo of the paper. This time it was much easier to do: I didn’t have to defeat the case closed switch; there’s a convenient diagnostic option in the Form Studio 1 menu for enabling this!

Here’s what it looks like on the new Form Studio 1:

Here’s what it looked like on the Form 4:

Despite the cost-down, the light uniformity looks great! Now, let’s have a look inside and see what’s changed.

I decided that the back panel was probably the right place to start – either that or the tank cover was the last thing attached, so it’d be the first thing to take off.

A few screws later, and the back side is revealed. The most notable feature is a pair of tubes going from the frame to the back panel.

I originally guessed these were for air circulation of some type, but upon consultation with Formlabs they informed me that the tubes are for facilitating the drainage of spilled resin. Makes sense, now that I think about it – if the thin film that forms the bottom of the resin tank failed for any reason, it’d be a spill-pocalypse!

A few more screws later, and the bottom plate and air filter are removed, revealing what is primarily the heat sink assembly for the actual light source.

The bottom cover itself has something very curious about it.

The bottom cover has a pattern of air holes in it that are decidedly not regular, and not random. I thought this was an Easter egg of some type. I pondered it manually, and then I tried image processing it and throwing it into my machine to suggest other ideas, but still came up with nothing.

One reason I strongly suspected there was a message is that I did this once upon a time in one of my products. The NeTV2 hid a coded message in its cooling holes:

To the best of my knowledge, nobody ever figured this one out. The message is actually pretty easy to decode – if you want to give it a try yourself, I’ve hidden the decode method and answer as a “spoilers” tag:

Unfortunately, upon consultation with Formlabs, the pattern of holes was an Easter egg – it was just the pattern they came up with to adequately cool various systems in the printer. Still pretty interesting to think about from that perspective. I wonder how they picked where to put the holes? A simulation of airflow? Some empirical measurements with a smoke machine, mapping out airflow? It’s perhaps even more curious that the pattern was deliberate and optimized; I wonder how they did it!

The light source on the Form Studio 1 is greatly simplified compared to the Form 4. The Form 4 had multiple individually controllable light zones; the Form Studio 1 looks to have just a single chain of LEDs driven by a much simplified controller, and an EEPROM to identify the assembly.

Like the previous generation, this is a single-layer PCB built onto an aluminum core PCB, for better heat sinking. Despite the simplification, the light uniformity is excellent, so this seems to be a cost-down without compromises (or perhaps the original light source was over-engineered).

Accessing the lens assembly is just four screws to pull off the light source:

The lens assembly is also simplified in the Form Studio 1 compared to the Form 4. On the Form 4 there was an additional diffuser stage; here, the extra diffuser is gone and all the diffusion comes from a pattern integrated into the lens texture itself.

The molding on the lens is exquisite; a side view gives you an idea of the clarity and uniformity of the optical-grade plastics used in the assembly:

With the lens assembly removed (and a few more parts taken off, which I’ll return to later in the post), we arrive at the base plate with the LCD still mounted.

From this perspective, we can see how the base plate forms a shared reference point for the whole system:

  • The LCD is firmly attached to the base plate
  • The Z-motor is likewise attached to the same reference plane
  • The light box would extend back from the plane of the LCD

All this combines to create a clean, straightforward optics path with minimal degrees of freedom for offsets, with most critical dimensions set by two CNC operations on either side of the base plate plus the precision of the injection molds. This means the precision of the assembly relies less on the skill of the operators and more on repeatable machine operations.

The top side of the LCD assembly shows the embedded PCB trace heaters for the resin, required to maintain optimal resin temperature for printing. The texturing of the layer between the resin tank and the LCD shows some additional tweaks compared to the Form 4.

The back side of the LCD assembly, once removed from the aluminum base plate, shows both the LCD data connector and the heater power cable. Like its predecessor, the LCD cell itself is bonded into the frame, and incorporates a thick sheet of glass to maintain mechanical rigidity throughout all phases of the printing process.

Many of the other details of the printer – the resin level sensing, RFIDs, resin dispensing and camera subsystem – are largely identical to the Form 4. However, one difference of note is how the build platform is mounted. Detecting the build platform is not as simple as you’d think, because sometimes users can space out and start a print with the platform absent, or perhaps worse yet, with a leftover print still hanging off the platform.

The Form Studio 1 has a major upgrade in this regard:

The build platform itself integrates a load cell!

To review, a load cell is the heart of every digital weight scale. It senses minute distortions in a beam to infer the mass of an object placed on it. Both the Form 3 and the Form 4 integrated load cells underneath the resin cartridge to measure remaining resin level and usage.

On the Form Studio 1, the load cell is under the resin cartridge – it got moved to the build platform. So there is still one load cell, but instead of being used to monitor resin consumption, it’s being used to improve user experience. That’s a bit surprising given the general trend of enshittification – you rarely see a tech company transform a resource with real potential for extracting more customer revenue into one that genuinely improves user experience.

The load cell in the Form Studio 1 evidently measures the mass of the build platform. After the build platform is installed, there is a calibration step – that makes sense, as load cells need to be tared. Once tared, they can sense tiny mass changes. I don’t have visibility into the precision of this load cell, but they can generally sense sub-gram mass changes. This means if a print is left hanging on the build platform, the device should be able to detect it by comparing the calibrated mass of the build platform against the current mass. This is a pretty elegant solution to a hard problem, which also did not involve adding cost to the system because it’s repurposing an existing component for a new feature.

I asked Formlabs for their fact check on this feature, and they pointed out that the Form 4 was also able to sense forces due to a different type of force sensor at the bottom of the Z-axis; I had missed that sensor in the previous teardown. That being said, apparently a key function of the stir bar (properly referred to as the “mixer”) on the Form 4 was to detect foreign objects on the resin tank; since this was costed out in the Form Studio 1, the load cell in the build platform mount also takes on the task of foreign object detection inside the tank, as well as detecting misconfigured build platforms.

Remarkably, the electronics are perhaps the least interesting part of this teardown because you don’t even need to tear down the system to see most of the main board!

However, with the case off, we can get a clearer snapshot of all the part numbers. Here’s the right hand side of the circuit board:

The board is beautifully labeled: no notes on this one. This board was made to be looked at.

On the left hand side, I removed the heatsink on the SoM to reveal the components underneath. Instead of a Raspberry Pi compute module used on prior editions of the printer, this uses a Rockchip RK3568-based SoM by Forlinx configured with 1GiB of LPDDR4X RAM and 32GiB of eMMC. Given rumors of spotty supply and rising prices from Raspberry Pi, a migration to a pure-play SoM provider makes sense. One nice thing about using a SoM is you’re not locked into a given vendor – so long as you keep your usage of the Linux distribution generic and portable, it’s a modest lift to port to a new vendor and qualify the product, restoring negotiating leverage to the buyer.

The back side of the mainboard is completely clean – not a single component. This makes sense for a cost-down like this – keeping the design single-sided with no through-hole component removes several steps in the PCB assembly process. Automated optical inspection catches most of the assembly errors, and the plethora of cabling to driven peripherals means you don’t need too many additional test points to do a comprehensive functional test of the assembled board.

Not-so-secretly, I have an obsession with power supplies. Many system integrators reduce costs by cutting corners on the power supplies, and so this is one of the places I look to check if standards are being held after a cost-down. The Form Studio 1 power supply is provided in a tidy module that snaps into the chassis.

Taking off the cover reveals the internals:

This power supply checks all the boxes – tidy construction, all-new components, plenty of adhesive to hold components in place for reflow assembly, adequate heat sinking and modern architecture. There’s an additional layer of components on the back side which I did not reveal, because I’d like to keep this power supply intact and re-use it for my own projects after the teardown!

Another generation of Formlabs printer, another teardown! I’ve always enjoyed being able to take these machines apart and to learn from them. This one was especially interesting because it demonstrates growth along a new axis for Formlabs. Previous printers pushed the technical frontier; this one is a pivot into cost-down territory. This transition is often fraught with difficult choices, and I think they did a good job of picking their battles, simplifying the design, and taking a holistic approach to reducing cost while not degrading the user experience. The move of the load cell from detecting resin consumption to build platform presence is especially interesting, because despite going for a lower cost architecture, they removed a knob they could use to extract more revenue from customers and instead deployed it as a sensor that improves customer experience. The 3D printing space has become a hyper-competitive cost-sensitive race-to-the-bottom market, and the Form Studio 1 is a solid move towards addressing the realities of today’s rapidly shifting business landscape.

items.title: Name that Ware, November 2026
items.author: bunnie
items.content:
The Ware for November 2026 is shown below.

I felt a little nostalgic, as I always do around this time of year. I picked an easy-to-guess ware, but one from that era when I anticipated the holiday season the way a child would. This one was plucked from a trove I found recently – a board I distinctly remember being quite curious about, but which had been kept safely out of reach because back then it was expensive and my father didn’t want me pulling the chips off and breaking it (and apparently it has remained hidden there ever since!).

I find it interesting that even back then, some chips had their part numbers ground off to discourage cloning. Also, note the Foxconn-branded connectors, reflecting the company’s origin story as a manufacturer of discount connector clones. I think this board dates from a vintage when Foxconn was still mostly making connectors and only just starting to diversify into other lines of business.

items.title: Winner, Name that Ware October 2026
items.author: bunnie
items.content:
The ware for October 2026 is the control board from a SodaStream drinking water carbonation machine. It was really interesting to see people puzzle over the nature of the board – I would say I’d have a similarly difficult time guessing this. On the flip side, I also never would have suspected that the operating principle of a carbonation controller would be sensing the vibration signature of the gas moving through various valves and releases.

In retrospect, it does make sense – the sound the machine makes is unique and repeatable – so it would have a signature one could discriminate and trigger on. Accelerometers have several hundred hertz (if not more) sensing bandwidth – adequate for the task – and they are a low-cost, mass-produced commodity, thanks in part to smart phones anchoring their demand. Meanwhile, a microphone would pick up too much ambient noise and could miss signatures if operated in a noisy room. All in all, it’s a pretty clever solution to the problem, and the sort of trick learned by taking things apart. One more for the pile of tricks in my head!

Above is a photo that gives some more context to the overall solution inside the SodaStream. Thanks again to FETguy and Renew Computers for sharing this ware! There were many great attempts at guessing this one, but none were quite spot-on, so there is no prize awarded this month.
